key_insight: Finetuning LLMs on documents that explicitly mark a claim as false can paradoxically cause models to believe the claim is true; the same documents, when provided in-context, are correctly interpreted as refutations. This reveals a systematic failure to learn negation signals from finetuning data.
problem_solved: Identifies and characterizes a failure mode—'Negation Neglect'—where training signals that negate misinformation are internalized incorrectly, exposing risks in how models learn from corrective or cautionary texts.
method: Finetune language models on documents that present a claim alongside explicit warnings/labels stating the claim is false (e.g., news-like stories flagged as untrue).
Evaluate models by asking a broad set of downstream questions about the claim and compare responses to behavior when the same documents are supplied in-context (no finetuning).
Compare pre- and post-finetuning beliefs and measure generalization across prompts and related queries to assess how negation signals were or were not learned.
impact: Highlights a practical risk: corrective labels in training data can backfire and produce false model beliefs, so practitioners must audit finetuning data, label representations, and evaluation protocols to avoid introducing or amplifying misinformation.
visual_elements: Side-by-side Q&A example: model answers before finetuning vs after finetuning using the Ed Sheeran 100m example to illustrate the reversal.
Pipeline diagram: 'Document with claim + false label' → finetuning → model output showing learned belief, contrasted with 'same document as in-context prompt' → correct rejection.
Bar chart/heatmap comparing rates of 'believes claim' vs 'rejects claim' across conditions (pre-finetune, post-finetune, in-context).
Iconic visual (e.g., crossed-out label turning into a checkmark) to symbolize failure to learn negation and the risk of misinterpreted corrective signals.
paper_title: Negation Neglect: When models fail to learn negations in training
paper_authors: Harry Mayne, Lev McKinney, Jan Dubiński, Adam Karvonen, James Chua
